<reason>Both sides quickly agreed the switch must go, so the debate correctly narrowed to which fixed clock. CON built a genuinely good comparative frame — morning darkness falls on structured, reschedulable institutions while evening darkness falls on unscheduled life that nobody can legislate back — and its collective-action answer to PRO's "contradiction" charge (a single simultaneous legal reset solves what millions of actors cannot coordinate) was the best defensive move of the debate, materially blunting PRO's "mandate dressed as a clock" line. But PRO's pressure question forced CON to name a tolerable latest sunrise, and CON's answer ("around 8:30... Berlin, Warsaw, even Seattle sit close to that line") collided with PRO's uncontested figure of roughly 9:15 in Berlin under permanent DST. CON never repaired or disputed that number; it simply reweighed. PRO's closing exploited that cleanly: the case had to soften its own stated standard to survive its own chosen examples. PRO also kept a live, largely unanswered harm — chronic year-round circadian misalignment and sleep debt for everyone, not just twilight commuters — which CON only attacked obliquely ("standard time doesn't deliver morning light either"), and PRO answered adequately on dose-dependence. CON's rebuttals on the 1970s rollout and Russia's latitude were fair and partially landed, and its closing weighing was sharp, but the unrepaired self-imposed threshold plus the untouched biology cost leaves PRO the cleaner route. PRO's clipped second rebuttal is a real execution cost that narrows the margin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing use of CON's own answer to Pressure Q2: having been forced to name 8:30 as the defensible outer edge for winter sunrise, CON claimed Berlin and Warsaw sat "close to that line," which PRO showed was roughly an hour past it in the very cities CON chose to defend — and CON's closing reweighed rather than repaired the standard.</best_rebuttal>
